{"topic":"Power of Compounding","audience":"Aspiring Public Speakers, Content Creators, General Public","intent":"Inspire, Educate","format":"Anecdote","inspirationSource":"personal life"}

Compounding isn’t limited to money.

This is the power of compounding in real-life:

- The first time I spoke on stage, I was in class 7. 
It was a terrible experience.

Shaken by it, I didn’t step on stage again.

Until class 11, where I filled in for one of the class 12 Farewell hosts who fell sick.

That gave me the confidence to keep pursuing it.
I continued my practice through debating in college.

After 20 years of compounding, I have spoken at 450+ events.

- I started my YouTube channel in August 2017.

After 3 years, in 2020, I had 20k subscribers.
I kept making videos.

Today, I have 6 million+ subscribers. 

Habits are the hardest to build, early on.
But once they begin to work, they will change your orbit.

The pro is the amateur who showed up every day!

{"topic":"Book Lessons","audience":"General Public","intent":"Educate","format":"Listicle","inspirationSource":"a book"}

5 powerful life lessons from the book "Tuesdays with Morrie":

(The memoir is based on Mitch Albom's Tuesday meetings with his former college sociology professor, Morrie Schwartz, who was terminally ill with Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS). 

1. Relationships and love are fundamental to a fulfilling life.

Meaningful connections don’t just happen; they require time and effort. 

Achievements, wealth, and materialism will come and go.
The relationships you nurture will stay for life.

2. Live life as if it is your last day.

We think we have time with our loved ones and to do the things we’ve always wanted to.

Morrie said, “Everyone knows they’re going to die, but nobody believes it.”

Don’t wait to live the life you dream of. 
Don’t let it stay a dream.
The right time is now.

3. Don’t chase the wrong things.

What are you living for?

Is it money? Fame? 

Or is it a means to an end, like taking care of your family?

Find the meaning of your life and pursue that.
That is a life well-lived.

4. Forgive not only others, but also yourself.

Forgive yourself for all the things you didn’t do. 
All the things you should have done.

Regret is natural, but holding on to it will affect your future.
Free yourself from the emotional burden.

5. Your legacy does not die.

You will be remembered for the way you helped people.
The way you made them feel.

“All the love you created is still there.”

{"topic":"Teenage Pressure","audience":"Teenagers","intent":"Inspire, Promote Product","format":"Anecdote","inspirationSource":"personal life"}

When you're a teenager, everything revolves around exams and marks.

Not because that's the way you see it necessarily, but what the world tells you.

I was really good at Maths and Physics. 
And I didn't score as much as I thought I would during my 12th boards. 

I was one of the school toppers in English. 

And scored one of the lowest in school. 

Chemistry was my weakest subject and I scored the highest. 

I laugh at these scores today. 
Actually, I laugh at how I reacted that day. 

I was sad and mad. 

I remember reaching home and telling my parents, "Let's leave India - nothing is left in this country."

Classic teenager behaviour, haha! 

Today, I realise that those marks didn't mean much. 

They symbolised what happened in that 3-hour period and how the evaluator saw my answers compared to the script they had. 

If I could go back and speak to myself that day, I would say:

The true measure of your success will be your consistency. 
Not your starting speed. 

Life is a marathon. 
Not a sprint. 

Scoring low doesn't mean it's the end.

You will go on to do wonderful things in life, ONLY if you believe that you are worthy of them. 

We accept the life we think we deserve.

{"topic":"Overcoming Fear and Embracing Growth","audience":"Aspiring Writers, Content Creators, Professionals","intent":"Inspire, Reflect","format":"Anecdote, Quote Analysis","inspirationSource":"personal life, a user question"}

"Why do you have your blog posts from 2005 public?
Don't you care that people will judge you for who you were?"

Someone asked me this recently.

Whenever I look at my earlier work, I am always left embarrassed.

I was an amateur.
I was nervous.
I was rambling.

So how is it that I have never cared to delete or edit any of my previous work?

Because:

My first work reminds me that I started.
My first work reminds me of how far along I have come.
My first work reminds me of this beautiful quote:

"Courage isn't about being ready for what you are going to face. 
It is knowing that you aren't ready and yet moving forward to face it."

Here is something you already know of:

Your first work will not be your best.
Your first work will leave you embarrassed.
Your first work will make people laugh, cringe, judge or mock you.

And yet, until there is no first work, there is going to be no other work!

Don't ask yourself, "Am I ready to start?"
Ask yourself, "Am I ready to improve?"

{"topic":"Redefining Success","audience":"General Public","intent":"Inspire","format":"Reflective Anecdote","inspirationSource":"personal life"}

While growing up, I believed that getting into IIT was the ONLY way to be successful.

Going out of India to settle was the ONLY way to be successful.

Working 16-20 hrs a day was the ONLY way to be successful.

Building a unicorn startup was the ONLY way to be successful.

But what if it's not what our life needs?
What if it doesn't work out?
What if there's something better we aren't yet aware of?

Is it worth losing our happiness to that one thing?

Today, I am wiser.

I know none of these are mandatory for success, and certainly not the only ways one can be successful.

Today, I am successful because I feel successful.
Because I am happy.
Because I have enough!

Your life is happening now.

Not someday.
Not when.

Now.

The more conditions you place on life, the more excuses you'll give yourself to not live fully.

Happiness is not a destination.
It's a choice!

{"topic":"Hustle story","audience":"Students, Entrepreneurs, Aspiring Founders","intent":"Inspire, Reflect","format":"Anecdote","inspirationSource":"personal life"}

I didn’t have the money to buy a laptop. 
But I had an idea, eBay, and a jugaadu attitude!

2002.

I was 23.
Studying in the US on a 100% scholarship.

Which was enough to pay for my living, but not enough to buy a laptop.

So I had to get creative.

During a summer trip back home to India, I discovered something interesting:

Physics textbooks that cost ₹400 in India were selling for ₹4,000 in the US.
(Due to them being Asian editions).

I went to Nai Sadak: a huge book market in Old Delhi.
Filled an entire suitcase with physics books!

When I returned, I listed them on eBay at a price that was still a steal for US students — around ₹1,500.

Sold out within 2 weeks!

I earned $1,000.
And that’s how I bought my first laptop :)

Necessity is indeed the mother of invention.

This is one of my favourite hustle stories from my life.
I’d love to know yours in the comments.

{"topic":"Personal Development","audience":"Working Professionals, Students","intent":"Educate, Inspire","format":"Listicle","inspirationSource":"personal life"}

School taught us facts. 
Life teaches us how to think.

These 8 visuals will reprogram how you work, rest, and lead.
To help you unlearn what doesn’t serve you, and lean into what does.

(Credit: Marloes Huijsmans for the brilliant illustrations)

They’re a reminder that:
- Consistency beats raw talent in the long run
- Rest isn’t a weakness; it’s a strategy
- Kindness and clarity are underrated superpowers
- Thinking clearly is a skill you must train
- Progress is built on small, deliberate steps, not just big wins

Which one did you need to see the most?

{"topic":"Education System Critique and Guidance","audience":"Teenagers","intent":"Educate, Promote Product","format":"Anecdote","inspirationSource":"personal life"}

School teaches you about mitochondria and the Pythagorean theorem, which is 90% useless.

But no one tells you how to handle failure.
How to build a career.
How to stop overthinking that one text you sent at 2 a.m.

No one tells you how to make decisions, how to process failure or how to build a successful life.

School teaches you about life like everything else: one-dimensional and theoretical.
But real life doesn't work like that.

It's complicated, and has several ifs-and-buts.

That's why I wrote a practical guide for teenagers.
To help them navigate and make sense of life the way I wish someone helped me.

Beyond the Syllabus: my newest book for teenagers launching 25th July.

{"topic":"Personal Growth","audience":"General Public","intent":"Inspire","format":"Reflection","inspirationSource":"personal life"}

We're told success should always be visible. 
Constantly shared.

But growth isn’t a performance.
It’s a journey involving different versions of yourself.

There’s something peaceful about it:
Waking up, doing the work, building trust with yourself.

You don’t have to post it to prove it.

Do you agree?
